_comment: The whole voiceover script. Each scene is a list of lines; each line is one caption and one voice clip. `speech` (optional) is what the voice says when it should differ from the caption. `pad` (optional) adds extra seconds after the line so an animation can finish. Scene ids must match SCENE_COMPONENTS in src/CnnVideo.tsx.

lines.text: How does a computer recognize a cat in a photo?
Most of the time, the answer is a convolutional neural network, or CNN.
Let's build one up, piece by piece.
To a computer, an image is just a grid of numbers.
Each pixel stores a brightness, from 0 for black to 1 for white.
lines.speech: Each pixel stores a brightness, from zero for black, to one for white.

lines.text: A color image stacks three of these grids: red, green and blue.
We could flatten the grid into one long list and feed it to an ordinary neural network.
But even a small 224 × 224 color photo has over 150 thousand numbers.
lines.speech: But even a small, two twenty four by two twenty four color photo, has over a hundred and fifty thousand numbers.

lines.text: Connect each one to just 1,000 neurons, and the first layer alone needs 150 million weights.
lines.speech: Connect each one to just a thousand neurons, and the first layer alone needs a hundred and fifty million weights.

lines.text: Worse, flattening forgets which pixels are neighbors, so a cat in the corner looks nothing like a cat in the center.
A CNN solves this with a small sliding window, called a filter or kernel.
This 3 × 3 kernel holds just nine weights.
lines.speech: This three by three kernel holds just nine weights.

lines.text: Place it on the image, multiply each pixel by the weight on top of it, and add everything up.
That sum becomes one pixel of a new image, called a feature map.
Then slide the kernel one step and repeat, across the whole image.
This kernel lights up wherever dark meets bright. It is a vertical edge detector.
Notice that the same nine weights are reused at every position.
This is weight sharing: a handful of weights instead of millions, and a pattern is found wherever it appears.
A real layer uses many filters at once, each looking for a different pattern.
Their feature maps stack into a new volume, with one channel per filter.
Two settings control the size of the output.
Stride is how far the kernel jumps each step. A stride of 2 roughly halves the output.
lines.speech: Stride is how far the kernel jumps each step. A stride of two, roughly halves the output.

lines.text: Padding adds a border of zeros, so the output keeps the input's size, and edge pixels count too.
After each convolution comes an activation function, usually ReLU.
lines.speech: After each convolution comes an activation function, usually, ray-loo.

lines.text: It keeps positive values and turns every negative value into zero.
Without this non-linearity, stacked layers would collapse into one simple linear function.
Next, a pooling layer shrinks the feature map.
Max pooling looks at each 2 × 2 block and keeps only the largest value.
lines.speech: Max pooling looks at each two by two block, and keeps only the largest value.

lines.text: The map gets four times smaller, keeps its strongest signals, and cares less about small shifts.
Now stack these blocks: convolution, ReLU, pooling, again and again.
lines.speech: Now stack these blocks: convolution, ray-loo, pooling, again and again.

lines.text: Early layers detect simple edges and colors.
Middle layers combine them into textures and shapes, like eyes or ears.
Deep layers respond to whole objects, like a cat's face.
Going deeper, the maps get smaller, but the number of channels grows.
Here is the full architecture.
The input image flows through convolution and pooling blocks that extract features.
The final volume is flattened into one long vector.
Fully connected layers combine all of that evidence.
And a softmax turns the scores into probabilities: here, 92% cat.
lines.speech: And a softmax turns the scores into probabilities. Here, ninety two percent, cat.

lines.text: But where do the filter weights come from? Nobody writes them by hand.
During training, the network makes a guess and a loss function measures how wrong it is.
Backpropagation then nudges every weight a little, to make the error smaller.
After many thousands of examples, the filters become edge detectors and object detectors on their own.
This recipe powers some famous models.
LeNet read handwritten digits back in 1998.
lines.speech: Lee-Net read handwritten digits back in nineteen ninety eight.

lines.text: AlexNet won ImageNet in 2012 and kicked off the deep learning boom.
lines.speech: Alex-Net won Image-Net in twenty twelve, and kicked off the deep learning boom.

lines.text: VGG went deeper with small 3 × 3 filters, and ResNet added skip connections to train over 100 layers.
lines.speech: V G G went deeper with small three by three filters. And Res-Net added skip connections, to train over a hundred layers.

lines.text: To recap: convolution finds local patterns, ReLU adds non-linearity, pooling shrinks, and fully connected layers decide.
lines.speech: To recap. Convolution finds local patterns. Ray-loo adds non-linearity. Pooling shrinks. And fully connected layers decide.

lines.text: That's a convolutional neural network.
